cards.front: What is ownership (DOMINIUM) in Roman law?
cards.back:
The property right giving the owner (DOMINUS) exclusive control over a thing.
• Also called PROPRIETAS; jurists also say SUUM EST ("it is his").
• § 354 ABGB: use substance and uses at will, exclude all others.

cards.front: Ownership vs possession — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Possession is a fact (intentional factual control); ownership is the right to have the thing.
• Possession needs factual control plus intent to possess like an owner.
• The possessor merely WANTS the thing; the owner is ENTITLED to it.

cards.front: Interdicts vs REI VINDICATIO — what does each give the owner?
cards.back:
Interdicts protect possession temporarily; the REI VINDICATIO settles ownership once and for all.
• Interdicts: for the IUSTUS POSSESSOR against interference and seizure.
• REI VINDICATIO: owner reclaims his thing from any possessor (cf § 366 ABGB).

cards.front: Ownership vs limited rights in rem (IURA IN RE ALIENA)?
cards.back:
Ownership is the full right in rem; limited rights give only partial use of another's thing.
• Examples: servitude (SERVITUS), pledge (PIGNUS), right to build (SUPERFICIARIUS).
• Owner must tolerate the holder; otherwise he may exclude everyone.

cards.front: What powers does the owner have?
cards.back:
He may use, exploit and dispose of the thing and exclude all others.
• Use it, exclude others, take all fruits.
• Modify or destroy it; grant limited rights (pledge, servitude).
• Alienate, authorise others to dispose, derelinquish, free slaves (MANUMISSIO).

cards.front: What are fruits? FRUCTUS NATURALES vs FRUCTUS CIVILES?
cards.back:
Fruits are periodic yields from an object's designated use; they primarily belong to the owner.
• NATURALES: derived by natural means, e.g. fruit and vegetables.
• CIVILES: arise from legal transactions, e.g. rent from a lease.

cards.front: What is dereliction and what becomes of the thing?
cards.back:
The owner voluntarily gives up possession with the evident intent to give up ownership.
• The thing becomes an ownerless RES DERELICTA.
• Anyone may then acquire it by OCCUPATIO.

cards.front: What is IUS COGENS and how does it limit ownership?
cards.back:
Mandatory law that private agreement cannot supersede; the owner exercises his rights only within it.
• Example: donations between spouses were forbidden.
• Example: Augustus banned buildings higher than 70 feet.

cards.front: What is the CAUTIO DAMNI INFECTI?
cards.back:
Security neighbours can demand from an owner whose decaying building threatens their buildings.
• Owners must ensure their property does not harm others.
• Neighbour restrictions resembling servitudes are called "legal servitudes".

cards.front: NIHIL COMMUNE HABET PROPRIETAS CUM POSSESSIONE — meaning and source?
cards.back:
Ulpianus D 41.2.12.1: ownership and possession have nothing in common.
• True: possession is a fact, ownership a right.
• Exaggerated: the owner usually also possesses and can use interdicts.

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about ownership — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Who is owner — and is the issue ownership or mere possession?
• Full ownership or a limited right in rem (IURA IN RE ALIENA)?
• Which power is exercised, and does IUS COGENS limit it?
• Joint owners (CONSORTIUM/CONDOMINIUM)? Remedy: REI VINDICATIO or interdict?

cards.front: Which two forms of joint ownership does Roman law recognise?
cards.back:
The old civil-law CONSORTIUM ERCTO NON CITO and classical CONDOMINIUM.
• CONSORTIUM: community of heirs, property undivided, no shares.
• CONDOMINIUM (COMMUNIO PRO INDIVISO): each co-owner holds a quota.

cards.front: What is the CONSORTIUM ERCTO NON CITO (Gaius Inst 3.154a–b)?
cards.back:
Ancient community of SUI HEREDES after the PATER FAMILIAS's death, owning the estate undivided.
• ERCTO NON CITO = "without the property having been divided".
• No shares; one member alone can validly alienate or manumit for all.
• Ended by the ACTIO FAMILIAE ERCISCUNDAE.

cards.front: What characterises the CONDOMINIUM?
cards.back:
Classical joint ownership: each co-owner holds an ideal share (quota) of the ownership rights.
• Each may freely dispose of his own quota.
• Disposing of the whole needs all; alone it affects only his share.
• Can arise by contract, e.g. a SOCIETAS.

cards.front: Leo and Irene co-own the slave Pamphilus; Leo mancipates him to Crassus. Result?
cards.back:
Crassus acquires only Leo's half; Irene keeps her share.
• A co-owner can effectively dispose only of his quota.
• Crassus may free Pamphilus only with Irene's consent or after buying her half.

cards.front: How is a CONDOMINIUM ended (ACTIO COMMUNI DIVIDUNDO)?
cards.back:
Each co-owner can sue for termination and division of the property.
• Divisible things (e.g. money): division in kind by quota.
• Otherwise: one takes all and compensates others, or sale and split proceeds.

cards.front: What are the three categories of acquiring ownership?
cards.back: By conveyance, by usucaption (USUCAPIO), and by "natural" means.

cards.front: Derivative vs original acquisition of ownership?
cards.back:
Derivative derives from the former owner's right; original arises without the aid of a former owner.
• Derivative: conveyance — MANCIPATIO, IN IURE CESSIO, TRADITIO.
• Original: e.g. USUCAPIO, OCCUPATIO, ACCESSIO.

cards.front: What is a conveyance and which types does Roman law know?
cards.back:
A legal transaction by which the owner (or authorised person) transfers ownership to the acquirer.
• Three types: MANCIPATIO, IN IURE CESSIO, TRADITIO.
• Acquirer succeeds into the vendor's position — derivative acquisition.

cards.front: NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET — meaning and source?
cards.back:
No one can transfer more rights than he himself has (Ulpianus D 41.1.20 pr).
• Encumbrances pass on: a mancipated slave stays burdened with a USUFRUCTUS.
• Fewer rights are possible, e.g. reserving a HABITATIO.

cards.front: What is USUCAPIO and what role does it play?
cards.back:
Acquisition of ownership by qualified possession over a statutory period of time.
• Cures failed conveyances, e.g. non-owner transferor or missing CAUSA.
• Original mode; former owner loses ownership without any compensation claim.

cards.front: Which are the "natural" modes of acquisition?
cards.back:
Modes Gaius bases on NATURALIS RATIO (natural reason):
• OCCUPATIO and acquisition of fruits.
• ACCESSIO, CONFUSIO/COMMIXTIO.
• SPECIFICATIO.

cards.front: What is OCCUPATIO?
cards.back:
Taking an ownerless thing (RES NULLIUS) into possession makes you its owner — original acquisition.
• Examples: wild animal, RES DERELICTA, treasure.
• Diana kills a wild boar and carries it home: owner.

cards.front: Who owns fruits after separation from the mother object?
cards.back:
The owner of the mother object — except four groups.
• BONAE FIDEI POSSESSOR and emphyteutic lessee: on separation (SEPARATIO).
• Usufructuary leaseholder (COLONUS) and usufructuary: only on seizure (PERCEPTIO).

cards.front: What is ACCESSIO?
cards.back:
When things become inseparably connected, the owner of the main object originally acquires the secondary one.
• Former owner of the secondary object can claim compensation.
• Vibia's metal sheet welded onto Charinus's chariot belongs to Charinus.

cards.front: What happens to ownership in CONFUSIO and COMMIXTIO?
cards.back:
Nothing changes: each owner keeps his portion of the indistinguishable mixture.
• Reclaimed by quantity vindication (VINDICATIO PRO PARTE).
• 2 t of Gripus' + 4 t of Stichus' wheat: 2 t and 4 t.

cards.front: SPECIFICATIO: Sabinians vs Proculians — and the MEDIA SENTENTIA?
cards.back:
Who owns a NOVA SPECIES made from another's material was disputed; a compromise prevailed.
• Sabinians: owner of the material; Proculians: the maker.
• MEDIA SENTENTIA: reversible → material owner; irreversible → maker, who compensates.
• Wine from Simon's grapes belongs to the maker.

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: IUS CIVILE vs IUS HONORARIUM?
cards.back:
IUS CIVILE is the older stratum; IUS HONORARIUM is the praetor's law adapting it.
• IUS CIVILE: MOS MAIORUM, LEGES, plebiscites, INTERPRETATIO.
• Praetorian creation: bonitarian ownership, protected by ACTIO PUBLICIANA.

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: How is a MANCIPATIO performed?
cards.back:
Formal IUS CIVILE ceremony with eight people: transferor, transferee, scale-holder, five witnesses.
• Transferee grasps the RES MANCIPI (or a symbol) and recites a formula.
• He strikes the scales with a coin; the transferor stays silent.
• Result: civil-law (quirite) ownership.

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: HUNC EGO HOMINEM EX IURE QUIRITIUM MEUM ESSE AIO … — what is it?
cards.back:
The MANCIPATIO formula for buying a slave.
• "I claim this slave is mine by the law of Roman citizens…"
• "…bought for me with this copper and these copper scales."

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: RES MANCIPI vs RES NEC MANCIPI?
cards.back:
RES MANCIPI were the key agrarian production goods; all other things are RES NEC MANCIPI.
• Italian estates with buildings, certain praedial servitudes, slaves.
• Draft and pack animals: cattle, horses, donkeys, hinnies, mules.
• Provincial land is not RES MANCIPI (Gai 2.14a).

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: Is MANCIPATIO abstract or causal? What are its prerequisites?
cards.back:
Abstract but derivative: transferor's quirite ownership plus correctly completed formal act.
• No IUSTA CAUSA and no physical handover needed.
• Without a valid causa, the transferor recovers by CONDICTIO.
• Non-owner cannot convey: NEMO PLUS IURIS.

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: What is a CONDICTIO?
cards.back:
A claim reversing asset shifts that are not or no longer justified (unjust enrichment).
• E.g. after a MANCIPATIO under an invalid sale.
• Recovers the goods or their monetary value.

cards.topic: 21.10. Ownership — MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO
cards.front: How does IN IURE CESSIO work and what can it be used for?
cards.back:
Abstract, derivative formal conveyance modelled on the ownership trial before the praetor.
• Acquirer claims the thing; transferor remains silent.
• Praetor adjudges ownership to the acquirer (ADDICTIO).
• Usable for RES MANCIPI and RES NEC MANCIPI.

cards.front: MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO vs TRADITIO — key differences?
cards.back:
The first two are formal and abstract; TRADITIO is informal and causal.
• All three are derivative.
• TRADITIO is open also to non-citizens.
• TRADITIO gives quirite ownership only of RES NEC MANCIPI.

cards.front: What are the three requirements for acquiring ownership by TRADITIO?
cards.back:
Authority of the transferor, transfer of possession, and a valid cause.
• Ownership or authority of disposal (NEMO PLUS IURIS).
• POSSESSIO handed over: physically, BREVI MANU or CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM.
• IUSTA CAUSA (TITULUS) recognised by law.

cards.front: What is a IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS? Name the main ones.
cards.back:
A legally recognised ground (TITULUS) justifying the permanent transfer of ownership.
• Most important: sale, loan for consumption (MUTUUM), gift (DONATIO), dowry.

cards.front: Abstract vs causal conveyance (TITULUS and MODUS)?
cards.back:
Causal: the transfer (MODUS) works only with a valid underlying cause (TITULUS); abstract: the cause is irrelevant.
• TRADITIO is causal; MANCIPATIO and IN IURE CESSIO are abstract.
• Austria is causal: § 380 ABGB requires title and mode.

cards.front: Quirite vs bonitarian ownership — what does a mere TRADITIO of a RES MANCIPI give?
cards.back:
Bonitarian (praetorian) ownership; quirite ownership only after usucaption.
• Requires an authorised transferor and a IUSTA CAUSA.
• Bonitarian owner sues by ACTIO PUBLICIANA; quirite owner by REI VINDICATIO.
• Same content, different procedure.

cards.front: Iavolenus D 39.5.25: T, told to donate E's thing to Titius in E's name, gives it in his own name. Ownership?
cards.back:
Titius does not become owner: T lacked authority to dispose in his own name.
• Possession and causa (donation) were present.
• BENIGNIUS EST: Titius keeps it — EXCEPTIO DOLI against E's REI VINDICATIO.
• T answers to E (FURTUM).

cards.front: VENIRE CONTRA FACTUM PROPRIUM — meaning and use?
cards.back:
Acting in contradiction to one's own previous conduct, breaching the trust it created.
• Donor cannot reclaim his gift; donee defends with EXCEPTIO DOLI (defence of fraud).
• Used in Iavolenus D 39.5.25 and Ulpianus D 12.1.18 pr.

cards.front: Iulianus D 41.1.36 (1): A delivers land thinking he owes it by will; B thinks by stipulation. Ownership?
cards.back:
Yes: agreeing the transfer fulfils an obligation suffices, despite dissent on its source.
• Unproblematic if at least one obligation really exists.
• Some scholars: the shared purpose itself is a cause — CAUSA SOLVENDI.

cards.front: Iulianus D 41.1.36 (2): C gives money as a gift, D takes it as a loan (MUTUUM). Ownership?
cards.back:
Yes, per Julian: D acquires ownership derivatively upon delivery.
• No consensus on gift or loan — classical causa is missing.
• Analogy: both want ownership to pass without consideration.
• This common denominator counts as IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS.

cards.front: Ulpianus D 12.1.18 pr: same facts (gift vs loan). Ulpian's solution?
cards.back:
No derivative acquisition: without consensus there is no IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS.
• D acquires originally once he uses (mixes or spends) the coins.
• Before: C may vindicate; after: CONDICTIO.
• But EXCEPTIO DOLI bars C, who wanted to give.

cards.front: Julian vs Ulpian on dissent about the causa — and the link to modern law?
cards.back:
Julian lets ownership pass despite dissent; Ulpian, stricter, demands consensus on the causa.
• Julian keeps the causa requirement; general consensus suffices by analogy.
• Julian's view is the basis of the abstract theory (§ 929 BGB).

cards.front: Inst 2.1.40: PER TRADITIONEM QUOQUE IURE NATURALI RES NOBIS ADQUIRUNTUR — what does it say?
cards.back:
Under Justinian, corporeal things of every kind can be transferred by TRADITIO, by natural law.
• MANCIPATIO, IN IURE CESSIO and quirite/bonitarian split had disappeared.
• Basis for Grotius: the owner's will alone suffices.

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about TRADITIO — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Check all three requirements: authority, transfer of possession, IUSTA CAUSA.
• Owner, authorised agent, or someone exceeding authority?
• Possession transferred how — physically, BREVI MANU, CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM? RES MANCIPI?
• Consensus on the causa? Fallbacks: original acquisition, CONDICTIO, EXCEPTIO DOLI.

cards.front: Which three models of transferring movables do modern codifications use?
cards.back:
Consensus (French Code civil), abstract conveyance (German BGB), causal conveyance (Austrian ABGB).
• France: ownership passes with the valid contract (Art 1196 Code civil).
• § 929 BGB: delivery plus agreement in rem; causa irrelevant (abstraction).
• ABGB §§ 380, 425: TITULUS plus MODUS.

cards.front: Which Roman positions do the three modern models echo?
cards.back:
Each isolates one aspect of Roman law.
• Code civil: voluntarist reading of Inst 2.1.40 (Grotius).
• BGB: Julian D 41.1.36 — consensus on passing of ownership suffices.
• ABGB: classical causal TRADITIO (TITULUS and MODUS).
